## Answers from Marta (2026-10-10)

1. **Title:** Associate, confirmed August 2025. The CV's "Senior Architect" is out of date. Use Associate.
2. **Calder Court, 68% less heating demand:** modelled, not measured. The building hasn't been monitored in use yet; monitoring starts winter 2026.
3. **Calder Court, her part:** the concept was a partner's. She was project architect from technical design to handover — the detailing, the wall build-up, the site. The site must say that, and must not say she designed it.
4. **Kirk Street, her part:** not stated. She answered Calder Court specifically but did not describe her role on Kirk Street. Treated as an open point — see `decided-for-you.md`.
5. **A School That Grows:** a team of four. She did the structure and the sections. The six boards are team work; her specific contribution is the structural scheme and the sections.
6. **Tom Reid's photographs (Calder Court, Kirk Street):** belong to the practice and to him. She would need to ask both, and credit him if used. **Not cleared yet.**
7. **Practice drawings (Calder Court, Kirk Street):** the practice's property. She can probably show the detail she drew herself, but has to ask first. **Not cleared yet.**
8. **Cabin at Kashuby:** all hers — design, drawings, photographs, build. Fully clear to use. She did not separately confirm whether her father may be named or shown in photographs — see `decided-for-you.md`.
9. **Kirk Street outcome figure:** none given. "Church hall into six flats" appears to be the whole stated result.
10. **Audience and ending:** in two years she wants her own practice. She wants the site found by (a) people with an old house or a small plot, and (b) schools that need a guest critic. This defines the site's purpose and its closing move.
11. **What she works from:** the drawing set, in its fixed order — location, plans, sections, elevations, details, schedules — and the RIBA Plan of Work stages, 0 to 7. On site: the snag list.
12. **What she learned from:** her father's workshop, and a book of Swiss timber joints she has owned since she was nineteen.

- Her part on Kirk Street (she addressed Calder Court only).
- Whether her father may be named/shown in cabin photographs (she confirmed the cabin material is all hers, but not this specifically).
- Whether Brandt Lindgren (Gdansk, 2017–2019) should appear — not mentioned in her reply, no instruction either way.
- Permission for Tom Reid's photographs and the practice's drawings is not yet granted — she must ask both before either can be published.

# Fact sheet — Marta Kowalczyk

Sources: `material/cv.md`, `material/linkedin.md`, `material/images.md`. Each fact below is marked with its source. Answers from Marta are added inline once given.

## Who she is

- Name: Marta Kowalczyk. [cv.md, linkedin.md]
- Based in Glasgow, Scotland, United Kingdom. [linkedin.md]
- Registered architect, Architects Registration Board (ARB), registered 2023. [cv.md, linkedin.md]
- Self-description (her words, from LinkedIn "About"): "I work on buildings that already exist. Most of the carbon in housing is spent before anyone moves in, so the most useful thing an architect can do is make an old building worth keeping. I also teach, and I build small things in timber with my own hands when I can." [linkedin.md]

## Where she has been

- Gdansk Polytechnic Institute, BSc Architecture, 2013–2017. [linkedin.md]
- Architectural Assistant, Brandt Lindgren, Gdansk, 2017–2019. [linkedin.md] — not mentioned in cv.md.
- Clyde School of Architecture, MArch (part-time), 2019–2021. [linkedin.md]
- Field & Rowe Architects, Glasgow, Sep 2020–present. [cv.md, linkedin.md]
- Studio Tutor, Year 2, Clyde School of Architecture, since Sep 2022, one day a week. [cv.md, linkedin.md]

## Jobs

**Field & Rowe Architects, Glasgow**
- cv.md: "Senior Architect, ARB" — no date split given, just "2020 to present."
- linkedin.md: "Architect" Sep 2020–Aug 2025, then "Associate" Aug 2025–present.
- **Disagreement:** title. cv.md says Senior Architect; linkedin.md says Associate. See Q1.

**Brandt Lindgren, Gdansk** — Architectural Assistant, 2017–2019. [linkedin.md only; absent from cv.md]

## Projects

**Calder Court, Glasgow**
- Retrofit of 96 flats, 1960s deck-access block. Completed 2025. [cv.md]
- External insulation, new winter gardens, 68% less heating demand. [linkedin.md]
- Material available: 14 photographs before/after (by Tom Reid, for Field & Rowe); full drawing set (plans, sections, 1:5 wall build-up detail); a diagram of heating demand before/after. [images.md]
- Open: whose result the 68% is (firm's/team's modelled figure, or tied to her role specifically), and what she did on this project. See Q2, Q3.

**Kirk Street, Glasgow**
- Church hall converted to six flats. Completed 2023. [cv.md]
- Material available: 8 photographs (Tom Reid again); section drawing through the hall. [images.md]
- Open: her part in this project; no outcome figure given. See Q3.

**A School That Grows**
- Competition entry, Scottish Timber Schools competition, shortlisted 2024. [cv.md, linkedin.md]
- Material available: six A1 competition boards. [images.md]
- Open: individual or team entry, and her part in it. See Q4.

**Cabin at Kashuby, Poland** (own work, not through Field & Rowe)
- 28 square metres, timber frame. Designed and built with her father, 2021–2022. [cv.md]
- Material available: ~200 of her own photographs, first post to last shingle; every drawing, all hers, drawn by hand then in CAD; a time-lapse of the frame going up. [images.md]
- Open: her father appears in this story and possibly in photos — see Q6.

## Figures

- 68% less heating demand, Calder Court. Source of the figure not stated (measured after completion, or modelled at design stage?). See Q2.
- 96 flats, Calder Court. 6 flats, Kirk Street. 28 m², cabin. These are plain counts, not claims that need checking.

## What others have said of her

- None in the material. Gap.

## What she learned from

- Nothing in the material beyond the "About" statement above. Gap — asked directly below (Q10).

## Pictures, drawings, files she has

See `material/images.md`, summarised project-by-project above. Note on authorship:
- Calder Court and Kirk Street photographs: **taken by Tom Reid, for Field & Rowe** — not hers to publish without asking. See Q7.
- Calder Court and Kirk Street drawings: made at Field & Rowe, an employer's work product. See Q7.
- School competition boards: likely made at/for Field & Rowe as well — ownership unconfirmed. See Q4, Q7.
- Cabin at Kashuby photographs, drawings, time-lapse: hers. No permission question, except that her father appears in the story (and maybe in photographs) — see Q6.

## Gaps

1. No outcome/figure for Kirk Street (only a description, no measured result).
2. No stated personal contribution/role on Calder Court, Kirk Street, or the school competition — all read as firm or team work unless she tells us her part.
3. No quotes or outside praise of her work.
4. No "what I learned from" material — book, person, first failure.
5. No existing site, logo, or visual material of her own beyond the cabin photographs.
6. No contact details (email/phone) in the material.

# Decided without asking

Marta said: "For anything I have not covered, use your judgement and tell me what you assumed." These are the calls made under that instruction. Each can be changed by saying so.

1. **Kirk Street — her role is kept general.** She described her part on Calder Court precisely (project architect, technical design to handover) but not on Kirk Street. Rather than guess a specific role, the storyboard will describe Kirk Street by what's certain — church hall to six flats, completed 2023 — and not claim a personal contribution beyond "architect on the project." Change: tell me her actual part and the copy will name it, the way Calder Court does.

2. **Tom Reid's photographs and the practice's drawings are planned for, not assumed granted.** The storyboard will design the Calder Court and Kirk Street sections so they work with this material if permission comes through, but will also note a fallback (her own drawn detail, the heating-demand diagram, the section drawing) in case it doesn't. Nothing gets built against unlicensed images. Change: tell me once you've asked, either way.

3. **Her father is named as a collaborator, not shown by face.** The cabin's build story mentions "built with my father" because she stated this herself as plain fact (it's on her own CV). But no photograph in which he's identifiable is assumed clear to publish — the ~200 photographs will be treated as hers to use for the building, not for him, unless she confirms a specific photo is fine to show him in. Change: tell me if he's happy to be shown, and which photo.

4. **Brandt Lindgren (Gdansk, 2017–2019) is kept, briefly.** It's a real early job, not sensitive, and dropping it would understate her training. It appears once, in passing, as part of where she trained — not as a project with claims attached. Change: tell me to cut it if you'd rather it not appear.

5. **Contact details.** No email or phone was in the material. The site will end with a contact method but the actual address/number is needed before build — placeholder only for now.

content.content:
1	# The concept
2	
3	The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.
4	
5	## What does not work
6	
7	- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
8	- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
9	- One 3D scene, however good.
10	- Another site's idea with the names changed.
11	- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.
12	
13	## Three things to find
14	
15	**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.
16	
17	Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.
18	
19	**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.
20	
21	"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.
22	
23	**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.
24	
25	The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.
26	
27	## What every form has to hold
28	
29	Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.
30	
31	| Role | Holds |
32	|---|---|
33	| The opening | Their name, and the question |
34	| Who | Who is asking |
35	| Where from | The places and the years |
36	| How | The way they work |
37	| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
38	| What came of it | Outcomes |
39	| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
40	| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |
41	
42	## What the object becomes
43	
44	In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.
45	
46	If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.
47	
48	**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.
49	
50	## Three concepts, each written like this
51	
52	Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.
53	
54	- **The question.**
55	- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
56	- **The object,** and its pieces.
57	- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
58	- **The opening and the close.**
59	- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
60	- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
61	- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.
62	
63	Then say which you would choose, and why.
64	
65	## Test each one before you show it
66	
67	Rework or drop one that fails.
68	
69	| Test | Ask |
70	|---|---|
71	| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
72	| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
73	| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
74	| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
75	| Honesty | Does anything in it claim more than the fact sheet? |
76	| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |
77	
78	## Three cases
79	
80	How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.
81	
82	**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.
83	
84	**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.
85

# The concept

The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.

## What does not work

- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
- One 3D scene, however good.
- Another site's idea with the names changed.
- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.

## Three things to find

**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.

Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.

**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.

"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.

**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.

The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.

## What every form has to hold

Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| The opening | Their name, and the question |
| Who | Who is asking |
| Where from | The places and the years |
| How | The way they work |
| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
| What came of it | Outcomes |
| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |

## What the object becomes

In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.

If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.

**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.

## Three concepts, each written like this

Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.

- **The question.**
- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
- **The object,** and its pieces.
- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
- **The opening and the close.**
- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.

Then say which you would choose, and why.

## Test each one before you show it

Rework or drop one that fails.

| Test | Ask |
|---|---|
| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
| Honesty | Does anything in it claim more than the fact sheet? |
| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |

## Three cases

How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.

**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.

**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.

**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.

**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.

# Concepts

Trade forms considered, that Marta named or that an architect works from: the drawing set, the RIBA Plan of Work, the snag list, the condition survey, the specification. Three concepts below use the three she named herself: the drawing set, the RIBA Plan of Work, the snag list.

The question, common to all three, drawn from her own words ("make an old building worth keeping") and tested against the fact sheet — it claims nothing beyond it:

**"What makes a building worth keeping?"**

---

## Concept 1 — The Drawing Set

**The question:** What makes a building worth keeping?

**The form — the drawing set, in her own stated order:**
1. Location plan — *the opening*: her name, the question, where she sits (Glasgow, Associate, Field & Rowe)
2. Plans — *who*: her own words on retrofit, in first person
3. Sections — *how*: project architect, technical design to handover — not "designer"
4. Elevations — *where from*: Gdansk, Clyde, her father's workshop, the book of timber joints
5. Details — *what*: the work itself — Calder Court's wall build-up, Kirk Street's section, the cabin's joints, the school's structure
6. Schedules — *what came of it*: the real numbers, each labelled for what it is — 96 flats, 68% modelled (not yet measured), 6 flats from a hall, shortlisted 2024, built 2021–22
7. The close — the answer, and how to reach her

**The object:** six to eight drawing sheets, true to an architect's actual sheet proportion, edge-on. At rest they sit stacked, like a set on a plan chest.

**What it becomes:**
- *Elevations* — the sheets stand up and line out side by side, like a building's elevations.
- *Details* — one sheet turns to face the visitor and fills with a real detail drawing (the 1:5 wall build-up, if the practice agrees; her own cabin joints if not).
- *Schedules* — the sheets lie flat and tile into a grid, like a schedule, each cell a real figure.

**Opening and close:** the sheets begin stacked and closed, title blocks hidden. At the close they restack, title block forward, her name on it.

**What it stands on:** the stated drawing-set order; Calder Court and Kirk Street as described; the cabin; the school boards; the figures as qualified in the fact sheet.

**What it needs from her:** the practice's yes for the wall build-up detail and the Tom Reid photographs, or confirmation to proceed on cabin and school material alone.

**Why it's hers:** the sheet order is the one she named, in that order, and the details chapter holds the actual drawing she did, not a generic blueprint.

---

## Concept 2 — The RIBA Plan of Work (recommended)

**The question:** What makes a building worth keeping?

**The form — the RIBA Plan of Work, stages 0 to 7, grouped into six screens:**
1. *0–1, Strategic Definition & Briefing* — **the opening**: her name, the question
2. *2, Concept Design* — **where from**: told as where the idea comes from, and whose it usually is — a partner's, a brief, a competition call. Her own origin sits here instead: her father's workshop, the book of Swiss timber joints bought at nineteen, Gdansk
3. *3–4, Spatial Coordination & Technical Design* — **how**: this is where she comes in. The detailing, the wall build-up, the structural scheme and sections she did for the school boards
4. *5, Manufacturing & Construction* — **what**: the work built — the cabin frame going up, the site at Calder Court and Kirk Street
5. *6, Handover* — **what came of it**: 96 flats, 6 flats, 28 m², shortlisted 2024, each figure labelled for what it is
6. *7, In Use* — **the close**: Calder Court's monitoring starts this winter; she still teaches one day a week; the invitation — an old house, a small plot, a school needing a critic

**The object:** eight simple timber-frame member cross-sections (a post, a beam, a joint), standing in a row like a frame mid-erection — the shape of the cabin going up.

**What it becomes:**
- *Concept Design* — the members lie scattered and flat, as raw timber before assembly, while the origin story plays.
- *Technical Design* — they lock together at a single joint; the camera moves into that joint, which carries the real detail (wall build-up, or the school's structural section).
- *Manufacturing & Construction* — they rise upright one by one, echoing the cabin time-lapse, until the frame stands.

**Opening and close:** opens as raw, unconnected timber. Closes as a complete standing frame, lit, her name across the ridge beam.

**What it stands on:** the RIBA stages exactly as she named them; her explicit account of where her own part starts (stage 3/4, not stage 2); the cabin time-lapse; the figures as qualified.

**What it needs from her:** the school's structural section drawing (hers to show, per her answer); the cabin time-lapse; the practice's yes for the wall build-up, with a cabin joint as fallback if that's not granted in time.

**Why it's hers:** the frame assembling from raw timber to standing structure is the literal shape of the cabin she built, and starting her own story at stage 3 instead of stage 2 says, structurally, what she said in words — the concept isn't always hers, the execution is.

---

## Concept 3 — The Snag List

**The question:** What makes a building worth keeping?

**The form — the snag list, as she described it: a walk-round, raised, checked, closed:**
1. *Scope* — **the opening**: her name, the question, what's being walked
2. *Walk-round* — **who / where from**: who's doing the checking, and what trained her eye — Gdansk, Clyde, her father's workshop
3. *Items raised* — **how**: what she actually looks for, project by project
4. *Items closed* — **what / what came of it**: each project as a snag closed — before and after, the figures attached
5. *Re-inspection* — **the close**: this winter's monitoring at Calder Court as an open item still being checked; the invitation to reach her

**The object:** nine or ten snag tags, hung loosely, red and open at rest.

**What it becomes:**
- *Items raised* — tags spread out, each showing a real photograph or drawing on its face when turned.
- *Items closed* — tags flip to green, one at a time, project by project.
- *Re-inspection* — one tag (Calder Court) stays half-turned, neither fully open nor closed, for the monitoring that hasn't happened yet.

**Opening and close:** opens as a loose hanging cluster, mostly red. Closes mostly green, in a tidy row, with the one open tag honestly left open.

**What it stands on:** the snag list as she named it; the qualified figures; the still-open monitoring at Calder Court.

**What it needs from her:** confirmation that "still open" (for the monitoring) reads as honest rather than unfinished; the same image permissions as the other two concepts.

**Why it's hers:** it is the only one of the three built around an admission — one tag that doesn't close — which matches a retrofit architect's actual caution about a modelled figure, not a chef's or a developer's.

---

## Which I would choose

**Concept 2, the RIBA Plan of Work.** It is the only one of the three that uses its structure to make the honesty, not just hold it: starting her chapter at stage 3 instead of stage 2 says "the idea isn't always mine" without a line of copy having to say it, and the object — a timber frame going from scattered members to a standing structure — is the literal shape of the one thing in the material that is entirely, unambiguously hers: the cabin. It also survives the swap test best. A colleague who claims concept design on their own projects could not use a form whose second chapter is about where ideas come from *instead of* their own concept work.

I've written up your answers and three concepts. Full detail is in `docs/story/concepts.md`; here's the shape of it.

**The question all three answer:** *What makes a building worth keeping?* — drawn from your own words about retrofit, tested against what you told me.

**Three forms, all ones you actually named:**

1. **The drawing set** (location plan → plans → sections → elevations → details → schedules → close). Object: 6–8 drawing sheets that stack, stand up into elevations, turn to show a real detail, then tile into a schedule of figures.

2. **The RIBA Plan of Work, stages 0–7** (recommended). Chapters follow the stages, but your own chapter starts at stage 3 — Technical Design — not stage 2, Concept Design, because that's where you said your work actually starts. Object: timber-frame members that lie scattered as raw timber during "Concept Design" (where the origin story — your father's workshop, the joints book — sits instead), lock together at a joint for "Technical Design" (carrying the real wall build-up or the school section), then rise one by one into a standing frame, echoing the cabin going up.

3. **The snag list** (scope → walk-round → items raised → items closed → re-inspection). Object: 9–10 snag tags, red and open at rest, flipping to green project by project — except Calder Court's, which stays half-open, honestly, because the monitoring hasn't happened yet.

**I'd choose #2.** It's the only one where the *structure itself* carries the honesty you asked for — starting your chapter at stage 3 instead of 2 says "the idea isn't always mine" without a line of copy saying it — and its object is the literal shape of the one thing in your material that's entirely yours: the cabin going up. It also survives the swap test hardest: a colleague who takes credit for concept design couldn't use this form.

A few things I decided without asking (full list in `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`): I've kept Kirk Street's description general since you only detailed your role on Calder Court; I've treated your father as named but not shown by face in any cabin photo unless you confirm one; and nothing in any concept assumes Tom Reid's photos or the practice's drawings are cleared — all three are built to work with your own material (cabin, school section) as a fallback.

Which concept do you want — 2, or one of the others, or should I pick for you?
